doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
title: Sidney Bechet and Johnny Hodges on soprano
summary: Mandel talks about Bechet's vibrato and mastery, Early Hodges sounding like Bechet, and why Hodges gave up soprano in 1940.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, they were Sidney Bechet horns.
Yeah.
Because he was popular in France at the time.
And Bechet could control it and really play it, you know.
Plus he had a huge wide vibrato.

I could listen to Sidney Bechet until a few years ago because of it, but if that vibrato; if I hadn’t listened to the vibrato and listened to just what he played he would have sounded a lot like Johnny Hodges. That was Johnny's main man.
Exactly.
But Sidney was really the first great saxophone player, most people don’t really realize that. Way before Coleman, not way before but before.
Several years before, yeah.
Yeah, I mean he really took charge on that instrument, I just couldn't go past the New Orleans terminal vibrato, it used to drive me nuts.
Well apparently he was a big opera fan, I think a lot of that was his impression of 19th century Romanticism.
Sure that's why the French loved him so much.
Yeah.

But I’ve been able to recently get past that and just listen through it like you learn to listen to a lot of things that you couldn’t stand when you were young, at least that’s how it was with me. And what the man played was just pure gold.
Oh yeah.

Early Hodges sounded a lot like that. You listen to Johnny Hodges on those Carnegie Hall things in the Carnegie Hall Concert with Benny [Goodman] if you didn’t know who that was it would sound a lot like Sidney except it didn't have the big vibrato.
Exactly.
Especially when he was playing soprano, that was just before he stopped playing it 1940.
Yeah, it was too bad that he quit.

Well he claimed that he was just getting too many, he was getting a lot of lead – you know Duke used to like to write that saxes high and light too which was the thing I was trying to do later on in the 50s with Elliott and he was giving Hodges a lot of lead soprano and at the same time he was giving a tremendous amount of alto solo work and Hodges just didn't want to have to deal with all of that, he figured he’d deal with one of them at a time so he chose the alto and put the soprano away.
